stem: A 14-year-old asks for help with “not making stupid relationship decisions”; she has started dating early, spends a lot of time home alone, is missing school, feels bad about herself, and has recently started drinking at parties—what is the best focus for follow-up?

options.text: Wait until she reports sexual intercourse before offering sexual health support
Limit follow-up to condom teaching because the other issues are separate from sexual risk
Broaden support to include sexual health counselling plus school engagement, family supervision and relationships, self-esteem and mental health, and other risk behaviours
Focus only on whether her peers are currently sexually active
Reassure her that early dating is not relevant unless there is already an STI or pregnancy

explanation: Broaden support is the best approach because risky sexual behaviour is influenced by wider psychosocial factors as well as sexual health knowledge. In this case, the follow-up should address sexual health counselling, school engagement, family supervision and relationships, self-esteem and mental health, and other risk behaviours.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because preventive sexual health support is appropriate before intercourse occurs.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because condom teaching alone is too narrow and does not address the broader drivers of risk in the stem.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because the best follow-up considers the broader psychosocial context linked to risky sexual behaviour, not sexual health in isolation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because peer behaviour is only one factor and does not capture the other important risks already present.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because early dating and associated psychosocial factors are relevant before STI or pregnancy occurs.
